items.title: How Gravel Tech Changed in 2026
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: How much has gravel changed in 2026? Here are the key things we noticed at the biggest races in the world.
items.lbText:
The Crux 5 stole the show in gravel racing this year, but there was a lot more to the tech than just one bike. (Photo: Logan Jones-Wilkins/Velo)

Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

The 2026 gravel season has come and gone, and I, for one, am tired. Since March, I have been on the gravel beat for Velo, covering all the tech and racing from the biggest gravel races in the United States.

It all started for me close to home at BWR Arizona and stretched out through the spring, summer, and early fall to Big Sugar Gravel in Bentonville just a few days ago.

While all this travel, writing, videos, and riding adds up—it’s also been a lot of fun. I have had a blast checking in with many of the riders, showcasing all of the new major gravel bike releases, and even jumping in the racing action a few times myself.

At the end of the year, it’s clear that while gravel might not be growing at the same rate it was a few years ago, it’s still the playground of fun innovation and tech that keeps me and so many others coming back. The pro side of things especially continues to be interesting. In gravel racing, the pursuit of top-end speed has proved to trickle down throughout the industry since gravel speed increasingly equals gravel comfort.

To celebrate the season that was, and to survey where the discipline is after a half-decade of professional racing in the Life Time Grand Prix, here are my big takeaways from gravel tech in 2026:

No matter how much some people argue, the cat is out of the bag: we are not going back to small gravel tires. Even on terrain with plenty of smooth tarmac, if there is enough dirt on a route to justify more than 40mm tires, the technology around tires has improved to where 50s are almost always faster.

There are a few outliers—Cobe Freeburn, for instance, has run 45s a few times this year, including his gravel nationals win on the Trek Domane—but largely it is now a choice between 50 and 55mm treads.

For general riders, this is a really good thing. The falsehood that narrower gravel tires were faster held gravel back from having more comfortable setups. This new “bigger is better” mentality just makes sense across the board, and I can’t see 45s coming back.

Last year, suspension had a moment. Throughout the year, gravel suspension seemed to be making a move to take over the gravel racing tech.

From a large portion of the pro peloton sporting the forks at BWR AZ, the first race of the year, to some notable testing that said suspension with narrower tires might be faster, gravel suspension seemed to be building momentum.

That didn’t continue this year. Overwhelmingly, racers cut back on how much they used suspension forks. At technical races like BWR AZ, there still were a few suspension forks, including Russell Finsterwald’s winning bike, but at events like the Traka and Unbound it was all rigid bikes and big tires.

I still find there to be a great use case for suspension on gravel bikes, even with this pivot from racers. It can effectively bridge the gap between cross-country mountain bikes and race gravel bikes. Yet, tires have gotten better, and weight still matters in racing. Looking forward, gravel suspension forks likely will remain a small niche within the landscape of gravel race bikes.

Even in the face of big gravel tires, there remains a push and pull in theories around gravel bike geometry.

For some, the goal is length, stability, and creating bikes meant to handle the 50-55mm tires of modern gravel in a way that resembles the tougher terrain gravel includes. Others are dead set on trying their very best to keep making road bikes that can hold 2.2-inch tires.

Personally, I find one of these geometries much more compelling than the other one, but many disagree with me. There remains a split, even among some of the biggest bike brands, of what is best. Ultimately, that could lead to some people having the “wrong” bike. But until then, there is more variety in ride experience than ever.

Speaking of ride experience, the last and perhaps most important gravel tech development in 2026 has been 32-inch gravel bikes. While this is not the year they have taken over, Cam Jones riding a prototype 32-inch Scott Addict Gravel—in the same year that Scott released a new 29-inch gravel bike—shows just how much attention the budding wheel size has commanded.

That will not stop next year. From sources inside the industry, Trek, Scott, and Specialized are among a large number of companies that plan to unveil 32-inch gravel bikes next year.

At this point, we don’t know when, nor do we know what will be available to buy. Nevertheless, what I can say is this is the last year when major releases won’t include 32-inch bikes. Over the next year, the whole landscape will change, even if there will still be 29 options.

While all of this is speculative, it has been hanging over the gravel tech landscape this year almost as if it’s an impending attack from the Boogeyman. Personally, I just find it all very exciting, especially as I learn firsthand just how powerful a tool these new wheels are to ride.

Thanks for reading and, most of all, thanks for following our coverage from this year’s gravel racing season! We will be back for more in 2027. Yet, before that, let us know what you thought was the biggest gravel tech change in 2026 and what you predict will change in 2027.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar ‘Happy to Be Alive’: More Spinal Injuries Revealed
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Tadej Pogačar gives first interview since Vuelta a España crash and reveals the full extent of his struggle since then.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar appeared on course to win the Vuelta a España until his stage 8 crash (Photo: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty Images) (Photo: Alexander Hassenstein)

Tadej Pogačar has revealed he was more seriously injured than first thought following his crash in the Vuelta a España , with not one but three spinal fractures caused by his fall on stage 8.

The five-time Tour de France winner said the extent of his injuries only became clear in mid-October, bringing home the risks he faced of death or paralysis.

“Two weeks ago, I was in Slovenia and I went to do another CT scan. I knew I had a C7 fracture, but then we saw I had two more broken vertebrae, the T1 and T2,” he told The Athletic , part of the New York Times.

“At that moment, I was happy I didn’t do the European Championships, which had been my initial goal.

“When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I’m just happy to be alive, actually, or just to be standing.”

The C7, T1 and T2 vertebrae are located in the lower neck and upper back.

Pogačar was leading the Vuelta on August 29 and looked set to win the race for the first time. However he hit a large stone on the road approximately 33km from the finish, landing heavily and suffering those spinal injuries, a fractured collarbone and a concussion.

He tried to continue but was forced to withdraw from the race. He was brought to a local hospital and assessed, but then things took a surreal turn.

“I was just laying there and signing autographs for the doctors and nurses, taking some photos,” he told The Athletic.

“I was kind of out of it, and they were cutting my skin suit from the back, taking small pieces of the jersey, and asking if I could sign these parts of the skin suit. So my skin suit now has a lot of holes cut into it which I gave to the staff.”

Pogačar returned to Monaco several days later and was cared for by his partner, Urška Žigart . Things were initially very tough, with the Slovenian saying he struggled psychologically.

“For the first two weeks, I was really mentally not OK. I was really down. I was not a fun person to be around,” he stated.

“I don’t think Urška was happy to see me around the house, because I was just, like, depressed. You know, just not feeling anything.”

Things became more complicated two weeks after his return when Žigart crashed in the Faun Tour Femmes and reinjured the jaw she had fractured in the Tour de Suisse in June.

Fortunately Pogačar was starting to feel better by then and, over time, both of them were able to return to training.

Soon after his crash his team said that his season was over. In addition to missing out on the Vuelta win he was forced to abandon his bid to retain his world championship and European championship jerseys.

Still, as the Euros approached, there were rumours that he wanted to make a return. The championships were held in his native Slovenia and, as he noted, the road race was ten kilometers from his parents’ home.

He knew the roads extremely well and was motivated to return. However a follow up X-ray showed that his fracture was not healing quickly and with his team not keen for him to race, he backed off.

He subsequently found out that his T1 and T2 vertebrae were also fractured.

That poised additional risks, particularly if he fell again.

“Because it’s not as visible as a collarbone, everybody forgets about it, I think,” he said. “People who have experienced it, or know somebody that has broken vertebrae, knows how serious it is. It was strange because it was not really painful in the position where it was broken, I was focusing more on the collarbone.

“But if I crash again on the bike now, it can be very problematic. Everybody says that I was lucky, and you’re always lucky after a crash where you can walk away and you’re fine. But the more you talk with people, the more you find out about the seriousness of the injury. You have the internet and you google it. You see it’s pretty serious and not to joke around. It’s a bit scary, to be honest, to think about it.”

Pogačar is back training regularly, although caution about his injuries and the danger of another fall didn’t stop him from being accused of reckless riding in Monaco.

He will continue working hard and even if the Tour de France race director Christian Prudhomme suggested that he might not get back to his previous level, will aim to have a superb 2027.

If he does achieve that, fans will be relieved that the initial consequences of his crash were not as serious as could have been.

They’ll also be relieved that he didn’t line out in the Europeans unaware that he had not one but three spinal fractures.

items.title: The Lazer Vento KinetiCore is a Top-Tier Aero Helmet. Right Now It’s 35% Off.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: I am always looking for the cheapest way to buy free speed. This is a great helmet and it's deeply discounted.
items.lbText:

When it comes to going fast on a bike, aerodynamics is the modern answer. Weight matters, but we’ve long since established that aero wins out. So just go buy a new aero bike and a set of deep wheels… oh wait, that costs a fortune, plus you might actually prefer the snappy feel of a lightweight climbing bike anyway.

There’s another option though. The reality is that an aero helmet can save as much drag as those 50mm wheels you’ve been dreaming about, and it might even save more watts than a dedicated aero frame. That level of free speed is exactly why I’m paying attention to this deal on the Lazer Vento KinetiCore; pro-level aero helmets rarely see deep discounts, making a 35% price drop well worth a look.

Lazer built the Vento KinetiCore to be fast, and it seems the brand succeeded. If you look at independent aero testing, the Vento sits right in the same tier as the MET Manta and the Kask Utopia Y, while not being far off the Sweet Protection Tucker. Aero numbers are finicky, though. You also have to live with a helmet, and the things that really set the Vento KinetiCore apart are the quality-of-life details.

Instead of adding a separate plastic slip-plane liner inside the helmet for rotational impact protection, Lazer molded its “KinetiCore” crumple zones directly into the EPS foam. Removing that internal liner leaves huge, unobstructed Venturi channels for airflow, making it breathe exceptionally well for an aero helmet.

Lazer also uses a unique “ScrollSys” treadmill-like belt on the back of the helmet instead of a traditional dial fit system. It sits flat, which makes it comfortable against the back of your head and very ponytail-friendly.

items.title: French Para-Cyclist Suspended in EPO Doping Case at Worlds
items.author: ahood
items.content: Thomas Peyroton-Dartet, 41, tested positive for EPO two days before winning a para-cycling world title. He is now provisionally suspended.
items.lbText:
France's Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has been suspended for EPO, the ITA reported. (Photo: Andrew Matthews/PA Images via Getty Images)

French para-cyclist Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for EPO at September’s world championships in Huntsville, Alabama, the International Testing Agency announced Thursday.

Peyroton-Dartet — a C3 category athlete — is provisionally suspended while the case proceeds. No final sanction has been announced.

The finding came from a sample collected September 5 during the UCI Para-cycling Road World Championships. The ITA, which runs the UCI’s independent anti-doping program , is handling the case .

Just two days later, he won gold in the C3 road race ahead of a pair of chasing Spanish riders.

Peyroton-Dartet, 41, also won gold in the C3 time trial and silver in the C1-3 road race in the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.

EPO needs little introduction for cycling fans.

It stimulates red blood cell production, increasing the oxygen available to working muscles and boosting endurance. This is not the first time that EPO has been detected in para-cycling.

Poland’s Marcin Polak received a four-year ban in 2022 after three samples collected in 2021 tested positive. His results during the affected period were wiped out.

items.title: Factor Bikes Returns to Men’s WorldTour With Major Bahrain Deal
items.author: ahood
items.content: Bahrain swaps Bianchi for Factor as brand returns to the men’s top division following its departure from Israel-Premier Tech.
items.lbText:
Factor is back in the men's WorldTour with its new deal with Bahrain Victorious. (Photo: Gongora/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Factor Bikes is heading back to the men’s WorldTour, and Bahrain Victorious is changing bikes again.

The team confirmed a new partnership beginning in 2027, bringing Factor back to cycling’s top men’s division after a season away following its split with Israel-Premier Tech at the end of 2025 .

Factor secures a place in the WorldTour and a guaranteed spot in the Tour de France .

“Personally, I find it fitting that Factor was born in the UK, and next year, in our 10th anniversary year, Factor will be back at the highest level of racing in the UK at the Tour de France,” said Factor founder Rob Gitelis.

Friday’s announcement did not specify details, but the deal means Factor’s aero-focused Ostro VAM and lightweight O2 VAM climbing bike will be back in the men’s WorldTour.

The company will supply Bahrain across the grand tours and classics with its full fleet of bikes.

For Bahrain, the deal means another equipment switch as its relationship with Bianchi ends and will mark its third bike supplier in as many years.

Factor’s one-year absence from the men’s WorldTour didn’t mean it disappeared from the peloton. Like most top brands, Factor’s DNA is spread across the pack.

The brand supplied Women’s WorldTour team Human Powered Health in 2026, and backed Modern Adventure Pro Cycling , the men’s ProTeam founded by George Hincapie. The brand will be co-sponsor for the team’s second season .

The Bahrain deal — which neither the team or Factor shared publicly how long it will last — brings the company back into the full men’s WorldTour calendar, with all the exposure, demands, pressure, and equipment scrutiny that comes with it.

“At Factor, we have always believed that racing at the pinnacle of the sport is fundamental to who we are. It’s where our ideas are challenged, where our engineering is tested, and where we continue to push ourselves forward,” Gitelis said. “We see this partnership as much more than supplying bikes to a professional team. It’s an opportunity to work together, to innovate, and to compete against the very best. We are incredibly excited about what we can achieve together from 2027.”

Factor previously supplied Israel-Premier Tech from 2020 through 2025, putting its bikes under riders like Chris Froome and Michael Woods. That relationship ended amid the controversy surrounding the team’s Israeli identity, that came to a head in the Vuelta a España as protesters disrupted the race.

Factor first entered the men’s WorldTour with AG2R La Mondiale in 2016, when Romain Bardet rode its bikes onto the Tour podium.

For Bahrain’s riders and mechanics, the agreement means getting used to yet another fleet of bikes. Bahrain raced Bianchi only one season after switching over from Merida in 2026.

Top riders like Matej Mohorič and Lenny Martinez will soon have the bikes.

The announcement did not specify which Factor models the team will race, or detail the wider component package.

Bahrain managing director Milan Eržen said the agreement means more direct input from riders and performance staff in the development process.

“We have found a fantastic partner in Factor, a brand that shares our performance ethos and our ambition to be the best,” Eržen said. “Factor is continuously innovating on the bike, with a huge focus on performance, which will enable our riders to have one of the best setups in the peloton.”

Work is already underway behind the scenes, with the team’s first pre-season training camps set for November and December.

items.title: Review: The Exposure Strada 13 RS Light Begs You to Ride a Little Longer
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The new top-dog from the UK-brand brings a level of ease to night riding that is vital to cycling through the darkest months of the year.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Headlights for road riding need to do different things for different people. For some, it’s just about the bare minimum: something for cars to see and to illuminate the road so drivers can spot upcoming potholes. For others, it is a key tool in their stable: big lights that power early or late rides that salvage exercise in the hectic pace of a busy life.

For most of my life, I have been the former. My headlights have been just enough to be seen in the dawn and dusk. As I have gotten older, however, that has changed. Lights have become more important as my time to ride has shifted to the early morning hours that are the bread and butter of Phoenix, Arizona, riding.

Lights are now essential kit that I have to think about differently. It is technology I need more from.

Exposure Lights has built a brand upon that attitude. The small UK-based shop has grown to prominence with lights that match reliable performance, long battery life, and sleek aesthetics.

Nowhere has this been more obvious than with the brand’s new Strada 13 RS light. As I have ventured deeper into the night as the seasons have changed, the Strada has been a fantastic companion in getting much more out of night riding.

Despite a size that is typically reserved for off-road-focused lights, the Strada 13 is a purpose-built tool for road riding. Chief among those features is the lights’ auto-dimming AKTiv technology.

AKTiv is automatically configured on the Strada 13 and is set to dim its beam when it senses an oncoming car. The AKTiv technology has been a fixture on previous models, but the new Strada has two sensors that allow for increased precision. On rides, this makes for rapid adjustments that keep my hands on the bars and the driver from being blasted by a few hundred lumens of light.

Speaking of lumens, while it might seem that the bigger light is there for more lumens, that isn’t exactly the case. Exposure does pack more lumens in smaller packages, like the Diablo off-road light. The size of the light is more for the battery life and the added road-based functionality.

That battery has been a huge plus in my riding. While I haven’t yet ridden through the night with it yet—which would certainly be possible for the Strada 13 on one charge—the longevity of the battery has been a huge benefit.

Compared to smaller lights, I have been thrilled by the combination of a powerful beam and the set-it-and-forget-it battery life. Through a full week of riding, with more than a few hours before dark, the light can stay on with no issues.

To put it plainly, 217g is a lot of weight for a light. Part of me loves a small, easy-to-add headlight for road riding. The Exposure’s Sirius 11 road light is a mere 90g, and it can still kick up to 1,300 lumens. Yet, it doesn’t have the same adjustability, beam range, and most significantly, battery life.

Previously, if I had the choice of a light the size of the Sirius and the Strada for the fast group ride, I would have picked the Sirius every time. Now, the choice is not so clear-cut, although if I were measuring my night riding time in minutes and not hours, I would still perhaps pick the Sirius for its weight and sleek size.

The other real wonky aspect of the light is the single-button interface. It takes a bit of trial and error to figure out how the sequencing of button presses yields the desired results. Even so, I find that I don’t always get the light to do what I want straightaway. There is a way to bring some of the light controls and displays to any head unit to make that functionality simpler. But, straight out of the box, it is less than intuitive.

The Strada is perhaps most useful as a piece of kit that is low maintenance, easy to use, and easy to swap between bikes if you have multiple mounts.

The light has two attachments, one for a 31.9-diameter round bar and the other for an action mount that can be attached to an integrated computer mount, and both are stripped down but sturdy. Both mounts put the light further forward, away from the bike to provide a better position to illuminate the periphery of the road. That said, with the added weight, be sure to check the weight tolerances of the mounts before using the light since it could push the weight limit in some cases.

All of my riding with the light thus far has been with the action mount attached to the bar mount for the Trek Domane I have been testing with. It has been incredibly easy to use, easy to set up, and the big light almost disappears underneath the computer mount and bar. Out of sight, out of mind rings very true for a big headlight.

Lastly, with a USB-C cable port, the light is always easy to find a charger for. It can also be easily flipped and used to top up other electronics in a pinch. While the battery might last a while, charging it takes much less time. With the optimal cable, the Strada will fully charge in two hours.

The Exposure Strada 13 RS is for two types of riders: those who ride at night multiple times a week, and those who will measure their time riding in the dark in hours rather than minutes. If you fit those categories, this is one of the best tech adds you can make to boost the quality of your rides. It is good enough to be that transformative.

To learn more, check out Exposure Light’s website , and to see more bike lights, visit our best bike lights buyer’s guide .

items.title: Who Really Deserves the Vélo d’Or? Let the Debate Begin
items.author: ahood
items.content: Pogačar and Vollering headline the Vélo d’Or 2026 nominees as new sprinter and rookie awards expand cycling’s most prestigious annual prize.
items.lbText:
Who's the best rider in cycling? The Velo d'Or prize tries to answer that. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Who is the best rider in pro cycling? The Velo d’Or prize tries to answer that.

The road season is over, but there’s still some prizes to dole out with cycling’s most prestigious and sometimes controversial awards.

L’Équipe revealed the nominees Thursday, with the winners set to collect their trophies November 28 at the Fairmont Monte Carlo in Monaco in a posh, Oscar night-style party.

Some of these are no-brainers. Demi Vollering will be the overwhelming favorite after winning a second yellow jersey and her first rainbow title.

Tadej Pogačar could match Alberto Contador as the all-time winner of four times. He’ll face off against the likes of world champion Brandon McNulty, French phenom Paul Seixas, and Vuelta winner Enric Mas.

There’s more hardware up for grabs this year, too. Four new awards will honor the best male and female sprinters and rookies, with fans deciding the rookie winners.

Created by Vélo Magazine in 1992, the Vélo d’Or – the “golden bike” in French — is cycling’s answer to soccer’s Ballon d’Or.

Winners are chosen by an international panel of cycling journalists based on wins, star power, versatility, and panache . (Full disclosure: I’m on that jury. And whittling down the winners can be harder than you’d think.)

But will Pogačar’s injury-shortened season undercut his chances of winning? Let’s dive in.

This one should be a sure bet. Vollering dominated every race she started, and won her second yellow jersey and her first world title.

Lorena Wiebes could pick up some votes for her dominance in the sprints, but she’ll be a lock for that new award. Spain’s Paula Blasi — who recently penned a blockbuster deal with Movistar — could be an outsider.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney — winner on Mont Ventoux — and Marlen Reusser are other contenders, but this one’s all but certain for DemVol .

A stand-alone women’s category was created in 2022, and Vollering could become the first repeat winner.

The big name missing? Defending winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, although she’s still in the running for the French women’s award.

Even with crashing out of the Vuelta a España and missing the worlds, Pogačar will probably win again, but his stiffest competition could come from within his UAE Emirates-XRG team bus.

Isaac del Toro and newly crowned world champion McNulty — the only American nominated — join him on the shortlist, giving UAE three of the 10 spots.

How to measure up Pogačar’s season? King Pog absolutely dominated the 2026 season, and only a superb Wout van Aert could deny him Paris-Roubaix. A crash doesn’t diminish his fantastic season, but his absence did open the doors for many on this list.

Mas brings a Vuelta title, while Seixas gets a seat alongside some of the biggest names of the past decade. Remco Evenepoel was unstoppable against the clock, McNulty won America’s first rainbow since the 1990s, and Van Aert could be an emotional favorite.

The classics awards give the one-day specialists their own moment on the stage, although there’s plenty of crossover with the main event.

This sometimes can get sloppy. With today’s top riders so versatile, it’s hard to pigeon-hole a rider like Pogačar into one category.

A few years ago, fans were outraged when Mathieu van der Poel was named best classics rider and Pogačar won the overall prize. Can that happen again this year?

All five men’s finalists also made the overall shortlist. On the women’s side, Lotte Kopecky and Puck Pieterse are hoping to win based on what they delivered on a single afternoon.

Women : Franziska Koch, Lotte Kopecky, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Puck Pieterse and Demi Vollering.

Men : Remco Evenepoel, Tadej Pogačar, Paul Seixas, Wout van Aert and Mathieu van der Poel.

The fast finishers finally see their own trophies this year. About time, some might say.

The new awards give sprinting its due, especially with sprinters increasingly seeing fewer opportunities to shine as grand tours have become more challenging over the past two decades (though the men’s 2027 Tour de France sees a revival of sorts).

Wiebes is the only rider on both the women’s sprint and overall shortlists. Matthew Brennan has two chances here, with nominations for sprinting and the rookie prize.

Women : Elisa Balsamo, Lara Gillespie, Charlotte Kool, Nienke Veenhoven and Lorena Wiebes.

Men : Matthew Brennan, Paul Magnier, Tim Merlier, Jonathan Milan and Jasper Philipsen.

Want an actual vote? The new rookie awards are where fans get their say .

And “rookie” comes with some fine print. Riders qualify through standout performances on their first appearance at a grand tour, monument, or world championships, so they don’t necessarily have to be first-year pros.

Paula Blasi and Seixas are also nominated for the main awards.

Women : Paula Blasi, Célia Gery and Isabella Holmgren.

Men : Matthew Brennan, Jakob Omrzel and Paul Seixas.

The French rider awards means the hometown stars won’t leave empty-handed, with Seixas appearing on his fourth shortlist of the evening.

Women : Juliette Berthet, Marion Bunel, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, Célia Gery and Cédrine Kerbaol.

Men : Dorian Godon, Romain Grégoire, Paul Magnier, Lenny Martinez and Paul Seixas.

For the main Vélo d’Or awards, each journalist ranks five riders from the respective 10-person lists. First gets five points, second gets four, and so on down to one point for fifth.

Sounds straightforward until you’re staring at the ballot and trying to decide who gets left off.

The ceremony will hand out 12 awards, including para-cycling honors, and will air live on L’Équipe ’s free-to-air French television channel.

I’ve got some decisions to make. Who’s in your top five?

items.title: Pivot LES SL Drop Bar Review: Taking Gravel to the Extreme
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Slapping drop bars onto a carbon hardtail might look like a parts-bin compromise, but for ultra-endurance routes and steep singletrack, 100mm of travel makes perfect sense.
items.lbText:
100mm travel fork Not as heavy as you’d think 2.4” tire clearance Dropper post compatible

Low saddle to bar drop Heavy Fork bobs and requires more technique than is typical for drop bar Lacks top tube mounts Boost spacing limit wheel and crank choices Max 38t chainring

In the search for what the future of gravel bikes will look like, one obvious direction is to take the concept all the way to mountain bikes. Half the comments already claim that modern gravel bikes are just mountain bikes anyway, so why not embrace the concept? The Pivot LES SL Drop Bar belongs to exactly this class of bike. The bike is a hardtail mountain bike with drop bars.

Pivot is not unique in offering something like this, and in the past, I’ve been somewhat of a critic of the idea. It’s easy to say this kind of bike is just a parts-bin grab. A brand has a bunch of unsold mountain bike frames, so what if someone looking at the numbers just sources a cockpit that will work? Now you’ve got a whole new category of riders to potentially sell a bike to, and investment is minimal.

If you follow that line of thinking, then you also realize the result will be a compromise. The Pivot LES SL is a lightweight carbon hardtail, and it wasn’t designed for drop-bar duties. The rear end uses boost spacing, so cranks and wheels designed for gravel bikes don’t fit. Good luck finding aero-focused wheels, and the bars that are specced are massively wide compared to shoulder sizes. Now that I’ve spent time with the bike, though, is that fair? Let’s get into my revised way of looking at a bike like this.

The best thing, and the worst thing, about this bike is the 100mm front suspension. In a way, I hate it, because unlike gravel suspension that often works as a set-and-forget kind of thing, the 100mm Fox front fork requires some recalibration. If you are used to something like the RockShox Rudy front suspension, this fork might bug you because it moves a lot. If you stand to sprint, good luck. It becomes a bobbing energy suck, and you are going to want to make liberal use of the lockout and adjustment knob. You will probably also want to adopt a much more mountain-bike-style riding stance, where standing to pedal is rare and you keep your weight back.

Despite all of that, this feature is what I like about the bike because it is, in large part, the entire point. If you prefer the feel and capabilities of a 30mm or 40mm front suspension fork, then this isn’t the bike for you. If you instead need the capabilities of an actual mountain bike, then you want that full 100mm of suspension goodness, and that’s worth putting up with the compromises. It feels like you can roll over anything that comes ahead of you, and this much suspension means better traction when you do it.

This fork is also what you want if you plan to spend days or weeks traveling across seriously rough terrain. Not the kind of terrain that a short-travel gravel fork can handle, but rough, rooted, and rocky singletrack across a country. You are going to be seated while pedaling, and as you roll over things, your hands and arms don’t have to be in a constant state of tension.

Now that I, as the resident roadie in our gravel bike Field Test, got to spend time with a bike in this category, I could also make the argument that this is what you want as a road-leaning rider. If you feel unsure of yourself when things get truly rough, then big suspension (for a drop-bar bike) is what will make the difference between always feeling unsure and really starting to feel capable. Just make sure you don’t expect to do too much mixed-surface riding, because that is not the happy place for this suspension or bike.

Although I mentioned some of the drawbacks of the 100mm suspension, I don’t really think that stuff is a big deal. You want that suspension because you want the traction. What actually does bother me is the lack of saddle-to-bar drop. It’s inherent to any 100mm suspension and fixing it is tricky, but if I could wave my wand and fix something, it would be this.

The reason it bugs me is that I want a bike that feels fast. When I really want to push hard, I am used to tucking in, getting aero, and just pedaling. In the case of the Pivot Les SL, it feels impossible to match that feeling because it’s so upright and the bars are super wide. Sure, I could swap the bars, but getting that long and low feeling is a bit more tricky.

The reason the problem exists is that 100mm of travel requires more space. The axle-to-crown length on a fork with this much travel pushes the front end up higher than a standard rigid gravel bike. While Pivot keeps the head tube as short as possible to compensate, you are still left with very little saddle-to-bar drop. Unless you are willing to swap in a radically negative-angled stem to slam the bars, you are going to be sitting relatively upright. It is a necessary compromise to fit that much suspension on a frame, but the result is a bike that feels incredibly capable in the rough, but somewhat sluggish and blocky when you are just trying to put your head down and crush a smooth fire road. This detail is why you sometimes see drop-bar conversions with bonkers-looking negative stems.

Unlike the 100mm suspension fork, I don’t believe this upright posture is really the point of the bike. While it is true that an upright position adds stability, if the bar and stem managed to get the racy position I like and I could combine that with the 100mm of travel, this bike would feel a whole lot different. It would shift the use case a little more toward gravel roads, but I would personally have a lot more fun riding it.…

items.title: The Coros Dura 2, Spooky Bike Stories, and Cycling’s Jorts Problem
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: We headed into the desert and it turned out it's hot. We talk about crazy winds and surviving the heat just to get to the climbs. Plus, answering your questions on aero math and looking at the new Garmin Edge 1060.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

This is a spooky week to talk about bikes. Logan Jones-Wilkins, Lisa Charlebois, host Mike Levy, and I (Josh Ross) are all committed to the bit, but we don’t let it distract us. We start off by diving into listener questions and chatting about why weight has fallen out of the top spot in specs over the last few years, plus reasons why you might decide to care about weight more than aero even if it makes you slower overall. Logan has some great insight here as to why the pros don’t care as much about aero as it seems like they should.

The big question still looming, though, is about our failed desert adventure. Lisa can’t stop thinking about it, and we continue to debate going back for unfinished business versus just letting it die. This time, we also bring in some stories from listeners.

From there, it’s time to talk about bike computers. This starts off with quite a bit of talk about who actually cares about an $800 computer with only so-so battery life. Pretty soon, the discussion turns to jorts versus spandex, and my hot take that the jorts crowd is the least welcoming group in cycling. Fight me in the comments if you disagree.

That’s not the main event, though. The real meat of the bike computer chat is the Coros Dura 2. We got a ton of questions about it, and both Lisa and I have opinions. My thought is that the ecosystem is really good and very important. Lisa cares about the vibes and is mourning the scroll wheel, but we both have plenty to say on what works and what doesn’t.

Which is good, because pretty soon it’s the Levy and Logan show as the gravel boys take on the new Öhlins GXF30 Gravel Suspension Fork. For my part, my hot take is that a well-designed gravel suspension fork almost never needs to be locked out. Logan seems impressed with the Öhlins, though.

Finally, we get to the big topic of the week: Halloween. We all share our spooky bike stories, and after you’ve listened, we want to hear yours too. Ever had something scary and unexplained happen on a ride?
