items.title: Life Time Unveils Standardized Qualification Requirements for Its Pro Races
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: Life Time is requiring all pro racers to meet a qualification standard before being accepted into its pro fields in its marquee events.
items.lbText:
Life Time has unveiled standardized qualifying criteria for riders looking to enter the pro category at Unbound Gravel, Leadville, and its other marquee races.

For 2027, riders wishing to race in the pro fields will need to obtain an “LT Pro Number”. Some riders will qualify automatically based on their previous results in Life Time events. Others will need to submit an application with proof that they meet other standards, listed below.

Riders only need to qualify once per season and are good to go for the remaining races in the calendar year once they qualify. Receiving an LT Pro Number is not a race entry or guarantee of a spot at a race; it only allows a rider to enter the pro race. Riders still need to sign up for each race. It is also not an entry into the Life Time Grand Prix; rather, it allows racers to enter the pro field at those events.

An LT Pro number will be needed to enter the pro field in the seven races that also comprise the Life Time Grand Prix. The Sea Otter Classic Gravel Pro Race, Unbound Gravel 200, Leadville Trail 100 MTB, Chequamegon MTB Festival, Little Sugar MTB, Big Sugar Gravel, and The Rad Dirt Fest all require an LT Pro number for the pro race.

The announcement is Life Time’s latest change aimed at creating more standardized, transparent pro racing qualification. Life Time announced this summer standardized qualification criteria for making the 25-rider fields for the Life Time Grand Prix , the premier offroad racing series in North America.

As gravel racing has become more competitive and faster over the years, Life Time has taken steps in the name of safety, including moving the pros to their own start times ahead of the mass participation rides. Now, Life Time is hoping that standardized criteria will make the pro races safer by limiting spots to top riders.

“We love that our events bring together athletes of all ages and abilities, and create opportunities for people to challenge themselves,” said Michelle Duffy, director of the Life Time Grand Prix. “At the same time, mass participant events like Unbound and Leadville are fast and can be tightly packed, particularly at the front of the field. Establishing clear, performance-based criteria for the Pro start helps ensure riders competing at the front have demonstrated the experience and ability to race safely at that level, while providing a transparent pathway for athletes to earn their place.”

Being fast doesn’t necessarily go hand in hand with being a safe racer, but the new criteria should help limit the pro fields to more experienced riders.

There are a number of pathways to qualify for Pro status at Life Time races.

Several criteria qualify riders automatically for an LT Pro Number. 2025 and 2026 results both count for 2027.

Life Time has denoted seven races as LT Pro Qualifiers, where a top result can earn you an LT Pro Number. The key word here is can, because you need to finish top-three and within 10% of the winner’s time.

Cutoff times for both LT Pro and LT Pro Qualifiers can be found here .

Racers can also earn an LT Pro number through these alternate pathways, though these will be reviewed by a committee and are not automatic. The committee is made up of Life Time race and series staff.

There are 19 non-Life Time events that offer racers a chance to qualify for an LT Pro Number.

In addition to qualifying with finish time, or a combination of overall position and finish time, racers who win their age group overall in a Life Time qualifying race can also apply for an LT Pro Number. Racers with an LT Pro number are not required to race pro and can opt to race age group instead.

You can read more about qualification and apply here . Applying is free and racers are allowed to reapply with every qualifying result they earn. Qualification is good for that calendar year, after which racers will need to either reapply or qualify automatically for 2028 based on 2027 results. You will hear back from the committee within a week.

items.title: Zwift Plus Review: The Premium Tier That Could Replace Strava
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Zwift’s new $10-a-month upgrade adds real-world video routes and an adaptive coaching engine that makes paying for secondary training subscriptions hard to justify.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Video routes mean more routes Lots of new badges to chase Quality machine learning based structured training system Workouts use group rides and RoboPacers instead of just ERG mode Immediate post-ride coach analysis on pacing and fatigue

Requires an upgraded Zwift Plus premium subscription When deviating from the plan feedback is unclear

Today, Zwift is launching Zwift Plus. This new premium tier pushes the monthly cost to $29.99, with a discounted yearly option at $299.99. In exchange for the upcharge, you unlock two core upgrades: real-world video routes and adaptive coaching.

Zwift considers this a massive milestone, which is why I recently went to Moab to celebrate the video-based routes ahead of launch. The concept was to ride the route indoors, then ride it outdoors to see how perfectly they matched. Unfortunately, we caught the tail end of a Pacific hurricane, so I only got to drive the route and ride it inside. Still, the big reveal ended up feeling almost anti-climactic—but in the best way possible.

The inside perfectly matches the real world, but you still get all the Zwift details you are used to. Zwift lays the graphics seamlessly into high-resolution and high frame rate footage. I rode the Tron bike in Arches National Park, and while it sadly doesn’t glow on the road, the wheels sit perfectly on the video road and the speed adjusts as you ride without ever breaking the illusion. It’s underwhelming, but only because it’s really good and feels like a natural extension of what Zwift already does. If you’ve used Rouvy, which Zwift now owns, this is better.

Personally, though, I don’t find the video-based routes all that much of a draw. They provide more variety, and that’s great, but Zwift already adds routes all the time and anyone who’s used Zwift knows the team is great at recreating real-life locations. What this launch is really all about is coaching, and that’s where the real magic is.

Part of why the team at Zwift considered this launch such a high-stakes proposition is that it’s a price increase, and that always comes with baggage. You could even consider the addition of the video routes to the Zwift Plus plan as a sort of tiered pricing structure where, all of a sudden, you have to pay for more routes. That’s not really true, but I can understand the hesitation.

I think part of why I don’t see that as an issue is because I don’t find the video routes to be the major news here. They are additional content, and as someone who will likely chew through every single additional badge Zwift offers this winter, that’s nice, but also not a big deal. Instead, I see this as a pretty clear value proposition of $10 a month for structured training.

With that in mind, my favorite thing about Zwift Plus is that I see it as a product that is going to consolidate the structured training market. I believe this will be a big hit to TrainerRoad, and I think that for many people, Zwift Plus will represent a net decrease in monthly subscriptions.

The reasons for this are pretty simple: structured training has to be good enough, and it has to create an environment where the user actually follows the plan. Before this launch, Zwift was mostly failing at both of those requirements.

Zwift already had training plans; they just weren’t engaging, they weren’t reactive, and they were widely considered to be not that great. With Zwift Plus, the first correction was the quality of the plans, and to address that, Zwift brought on Ryan Cooper.

If you aren’t familiar with the name, Ryan Cooper is the founder of Best Bike Split and the former Chief Scientist at TrainingPeaks. To understand why his involvement is so important, you have to look at what Best Bike Split actually does. It is a predictive physics engine that takes a rider’s specific power profile, weight, and aerodynamics, layers it over the exact elevation of a race course, and calculates exactly how many watts that rider should push on every single segment to finish as fast as possible without blowing up.

That is the level of data-driven modeling he brings to Zwift, and it is exactly why the brand is very careful to call this new coaching system “machine learning” rather than “AI.” Right now, AI is a marketing buzzword. When most people hear it, they picture a chatbot scraping the internet and hallucinating a generic training plan based on a text prompt.

Machine learning is different. It relies on math and datasets. In this case, Cooper’s algorithms were trained on the anonymized power and heart rate data of millions of Zwift riders, combined with peer-reviewed sports science. The system isn’t guessing or estimating based on what it read online. It uses actual machine learning to recognize patterns in your specific history, power data, and daily fatigue, and then mathematically calculates exactly what you need to do today to actually get faster.

This means Zwift has now solved the quality problem that TrainerRoad has so far always held as an advantage. But the raw quality of workouts is actually somewhat secondary in real life. You need not only quality workouts, but you need workouts that people will complete, and this is where Zwift has something no one else does.

Zwift controls everything about where you ride your bike, and that means the Zwift Plus workout plan has options. Once you set up your plan, the system will recommend an ever-changing variety in terms of how you complete a workout. My favorite example was actually the first day of the 12-week plan I started, when I was scheduled for a route rather than a set of intervals.…

items.title: You Cannot Pogačar-Proof the Tour de France: Winners and Losers of the 2027 Route Reveal
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Vingegaard is in trouble, Seixas wins and loses, and why we all lose without gravel. What the divisive 2027 Tour de France course means for the key players.
items.lbText:
The Tour de France threw a curveball at the peloton last week when it revealed its route for 2027.

The most time trial kilometers in 15 years. The fewest summit finishes in recent memory. Too many very long stages.

The route for the 2027 Tour de France is about as old-school as you can get, and one that’s already been labeled anti-Pogačar, pro-Remco, and designed to delight great French hope Paul Seixas.

But is Pogačar’s chance at a historic sixth yellow jersey really in peril?

And can we on the couch really count ourselves lucky that the Montmartre finale returns to stage 21 in Paris? We’ve got to sit through one of the most featureless parcours of the Pogi era to see the Tour’s monumental modern ending.

Here are some of the biggest winners and losers from the 2027 Tour de France course reveal.

The 2027 Tour de France has been called the “anti-Pog” Tour de France .

But there’s no such thing. You cannot Pogačar-proof Le Tour.

The controversial inclusion of 71km of flat time trialing won’t have Tadej Pogačar in a fluster as he plans his shot at a record-breaking sixth maillot jaune.

At the 2026 Tour de France, time trial topper Remco Evenepoel finished more than six minutes back on Pogačar. Assuming they both hold form into next July, Evenepoel will need to gain five seconds per kilometer to level with King Pog.

If you think that’s going to happen, I want some of what you’ve been smoking.

Jonas Vingegaard and Visma-Lease a Bike’s Killer Bees were stung by the Tour route presentation. The 2027 parcours does not suit the two-time winner, not one bit.

With just three high-summit finishes, next year’s race looks more like an “anti-Jonas” Tour than an “anti-Pog” Tour.

The course includes only one of the high-altitude, multi-mountain monster stages where Vingegaard typically thrives. The 18th “Queen Stage” in the Pyrénées is the only obvious place where the Scandi climbing goat might drop his punchier rivals.

Vingegaard can’t rely on making much time in the Alps and Pyrénées, and he’s not likely to take time on the TT bike, either.

The 29-year-old’s three-year wait to reclaim the yellow jersey might see a new anniversary next year in Paris.

Everybody except a handful of heavy sprinters won when ASO confirmed the showstopper Montmartre would return to stage 21 of the Tour de France.

After two breathless thrillers won by Wout van Aert and Mathieu van der Poel – two of the biggest names in world cycling – in 2025 and 2026, nobody wanted to see a return of the fusty old bunch sprint format in 2027.

Go block it out of your calendar right now.

ASO didn’t let us have it all our own way by putting Montmartre back on the parcours for 2027.

Next year’s Tour de France is one of the longest of the past decade.

Three stages nudge past 220km, three are close to 200km, and only the finale in Paris clocks in at under 150km.

Strip the two time trials from the total distance of 3,479km, and the remaining road stages average 179km in length. That’s too long.

What happened to the trend toward always-entertaining, super-digestible three-hour stages? Bite-sized packages of 120-160km seemed like the future for a sport struggling to find a new audience.

The weekend stages 8, 15, and 20 – the days where the couch, your snack supply, and the Tour de France are the only things that matter – are all set up as sprints or breakaways.

Oh, and that nothing-burger 20th stage? Don’t get us started.

Remco Evenepoel isn’t any more likely to beat Tadej Pogačar at the 2027 Tour de France than he was in the 2026 Tour de France. He’d need an act of god or some mid-90s “preparation” to make that happen.

But Red Bull’s “aero bullet” is without doubt in pole position for second on the podium.

Evenepoel hasn’t seen a route this favorable in his entire career. In fact, he was some teenage football player the last time the Tour de France was so clearly designed for a time trialist. “The Wiggins Tour” included a mind-numbing 101km against the clock in 2012.

Evenepoel should gain more than enough advantage over 71km of time trialing to offset any potential losses in the mountains. He further benefits from the lack of multi-mountain stages and high summit finishes that have proven his kryptonite in the past.

There had been rumor that Evenepoel will target a Giro-Tour double in 2027.

There’s surely no way he’s considering messing around with such a risky schedule now.

The Tour de France promo spiel suggests there are seven sprint stages on tap for 2027, but the peloton’s reigning sprint king ain’t so sure.

Tim Merlier has grumbled that heavyweights like himself and Jonathan Milan might see as few as four chances next year. And given the return of the Montmartre, there’s not even the lure of the Champs-Élysées.

Indeed, the 2027 route is tilted in favor of “modern,” versatile sprinters like Matthew Brennan or Merlier’s rising teammate, Paul Magnier. Accumulated climbing or late obstacles could cook the carthorses before they see some of the “sprint finishes” promised them in next year’s Tour de France.

The only consolation for the biggest, “purest” sprinters?

A strong chance at winning the first yellow jersey at the stage 1 grand départ into Carlisle.

The French nation breathed a collective sigh of relief last week when Christian Prudhomme released the route for the 2027 Tour de France.

The kid’s a monster on the time trial bike, and he’ll have plenty of opportunity to reinforce that fact next July. He also seems better on smaller, punchier climbs than towering high Alps. How convenient then, that there are relatively few of those.

Tour organizers ASO have a habit of weighting the Tour’s parcours in favor of its rider du jour .

And while we’re not suggesting that’s the case in 2027 – how dare we?! – there’s nothing on the parcours that might stop Seixas from bettering his debut fourth-place finish from 2026 next July.

But is that really a good thing for the 20-year-old?…

items.title: The Factor Sarana Proves Weight Isn’t Everything in Gravel
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: It’s not the lightest, nor the cheapest. But with massive 57mm tire clearance and a genius leaf-spring frame, Factor's ultra-endurance rig might be exactly what you need.
items.lbText:
Optional front suspension 57mm tire clearance Frame storage leaf-spring seat-stay system 52-tooth max chainring Available as a chassis only

The idea of the 2027 Velo Field Test is to look at today’s gravel bikes and try to identify the direction things are going, to figure out what the future of gravel looks like. Our choice for this is the Factor Sarana, and I personally could not be happier.

The Factor Sarana is designed to be an ultra-endurance race bike. It’s a category of bike that some people say isn’t real, yet it was the winning bike for this year’s Tour Divide race. It was also, realistically speaking, a bike designed with Factor athlete Rob Britton in mind. That seems like a real category of racing to me, and it’s also a category that actually applies very well to many other types of racing and everyday riders. Perhaps call it endurance gravel if that makes more sense to you.

The bike you’d want for ultra-endurance racing is, in many ways, an all-around bike. It’s not so aggressive that you can’t hold the position for days of racing. It’s a bike that helps you when you can barely think straight, and it won’t punish you if you get distracted. A good ultra-endurance bike is also a bike that keeps you comfortable over long distances.

If you are thinking that maybe a bike with those qualities sounds pretty good for you, you aren’t alone. Comfortable, predictable, and capable are perfect traits for most people riding bikes, and that’s why we felt like the Sarana was a good candidate for the future direction of gravel riding. I happen to be thrilled because ultra-endurance is my passion, so if that’s the direction we are going, great. Let’s talk about what I like, and what I don’t, about the Factor Sarana.

I have to admit that one of the things I love about the Sarana is that it’s targeting a part of the market that I really enjoy. Never mind that this is a gravel bike for a moment; think in terms of road bikes. Inherently, this is an endurance bike, and endurance bikes tend to lack appeal. People are not drawn to the sensible bike, so on the road side, it becomes an “all-road” bike—despite really not being that in many cases. What does a brand do on the gravel side? You can’t sprinkle in some gravel marketing; it’s already a gravel bike. The solution seems to have been to focus on ultra-endurance as a way to jazz this up.

That’s the most cynical way to view it, though. Instead, think about what ultra-endurance actually demands and how that translates to a bike. It also happens to align with Factor athletes, and that makes it authentic.

To bring this to a point: what I like about the Factor Sarana is the leaf-spring rear triangle design. What I’m talking about is a system that we’ve seen other brands take various passes at, but Factor is a company that takes pride in carbon engineering. Rather than employ a mechanical hinge like Cannondale, Factor started by dropping the chainstays near the bottom bracket. This design allows for the necessary space of 57mm tire clearance with a 425mm chainstay, but it also creates a curve that arcs gracefully up before finally curving down at the rear axle. Then, right at the top of that apex, where the design puts the most leverage on the chainstay, it’s intentionally flattened and thinned.

This chainstay design is also paired with a curved seat tube that has deeply dropped seatstays. That provides a designated flex point in the seat tube, with the seatstay positioned exactly where it needs to be to push on it and drive that movement.

This shaping results in a lot of movement in the rear triangle, but it requires nothing from the end user. By utilizing geometry and carbon layup, Factor created a frame that flexes vertically to absorb impacts while remaining laterally stiff for power transfer. You get a bit of suspension without needing to deal with the weight and maintenance of a mechanical system. Factor claims this provides an “18% reduction in vibration amplitude,” and Factor has also thrown a figure of 10mm of travel at me. Either way, the exact math doesn’t matter because the result is that you can feel it, and it’s just there without drawbacks.

This also plays perfectly with the 57mm of tire clearance. Bigger tires mean more suspension and more capability. Combine that with the vertical movement of the rear triangle, and you have this great combination of comfort and capability without dealing with the bobbing or maintenance of a shock system.

Weight. This bike is heavy. We tested the suspension version, and ready to ride (minus pedals), it came in at 9.58 kg (21.1 lbs). Of course, a large part of what some of the team appreciated while testing in Squamish was that front suspension. My personal take is that while the RockShox fork felt great when out of the saddle, I’d prefer the bike without it. Unfortunately, ditching the fork doesn’t fully solve the issue.

Even if you take that suspension away, it’s still a ~1,200g frame. In fact, we can do a bit of math: the rigid fork is 550 grams according to Factor, and the suspension fork is roughly 1,260 grams. In theory, swapping those out leaves you with an 8.87 kg (19.55 lb) bike built with SRAM Force—and saddled with a premium price tag.

To put that in perspective, the version we tested came in heavier than the 32-inch, metal-framed Salsa Fargo, and nearly matches the Pivot Les SL drop-bar mountain bike. Of course, our Field Test was designed to include wildly different bikes, so if we instead look at the Cannondale Topstone Carbon 1 AXS Lefty as a more direct comparison, the Sarana is slightly lighter at 9.58 kg versus 9.8 kg. However, the Cannondale is also $2,000 less and comes with SRAM Rival instead of Force.…

items.title: Sometimes Halloween Candy is Better than Energy Gels for Your Workout. Here’s Why.
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: We compared the cost and fueling value of popular candies to leading gels, and the winner seems obvious. But it's not always so straightforward.
items.lbText:
Cyclists who are sick of the frightening cost and ghastly gloop of energy gels should consider dressing as a demon and going trick-or-treating this Halloween.

The candy that will be dished out to expectant ghouls and gremlins this weekend is almost perfect riding fuel.

Kids’ favorites like Nerds Gummy Clusters, Sour Patch Kids, and the ever-controversial candy corn can deliver 10 times more energy per dollar and multiple times more flavor per mouthful than primo sports nutrition products.

But before you go craft a costume and muster a trick-or-treat patrol, there are a few things you should know.

They might save your candy-fueled bike rides from becoming a fright.

Carbs are the body’s preferred source of fast energy , but they’re a limited resource. The muscles and liver can only store a limited amount of carbohydrates, making it essential to top up during any longer, harder ride. Those who don’t face the prospect of an empty fuel tank and a miserable slog home.

Halloween candy provides exactly what the working muscles need: fast-acting, low-fiber carbohydrates.

At the basic level, it’s no different from the gels and drinks that promise to bonk-proof your ride with perfectly synthesized packages of energy.

And we all know the promise of sport nutrition comes at a price. A packet of “pina colada” or “birthday cake” flavor sports goo can cost close to five bucks.

When we compared the cost and nutritional values of nine popular Halloween candies to some of our favored gels, the results were not surprising.

A couple of handfuls of candy will deliver the same amount of carbohydrate as a leading energy gel, at just a fraction of the price.

For example, per our calculations, every gram of carbohydrate in a hyper-researched Maurten hydrogel costs 11 cents. One gram of carbohydrate from the Halloween love-or-hate candy corn costs one cent.

So that’s it, right? No energy gels, ever again?

Not all carbs are created equal, and candy carbs are not always the best carbs for workout fuel – no matter how damn cheap and tasty they might be.

The modern sports nutrition that enabled the high-carb fueling “revolution ” uses specific sugar blends to maximize carbohydrate absorption into the gut and oxidation by the muscles.

By using both glucose and fructose in 1:0.8 or 2:1 ratios, leading products allow athletes like Tadej Pogačar to fuel at more than 500 calories of carbs per hour, for six hours straight.

Try that with a bag of Twizzlers; we dare you. Maybe stash some toilet paper in your jersey pocket if you do.

Mass-market candy rarely, if ever, uses the glucose-to-fructose ratios that have saved the WorldTour from the explosive G.I. distress that once haunted high-carb fueling. Targeting the pro-standard 120 grams of carbs per hour with a packet of Sour Patch Kids will result in scenes worthy of the most icky horror movie.

If you hope to “train hard” rather than just “ride,” skip the sweeties. Invest in your workout and splurge on sports nutrition.

In many cases, energy gels and drinks are not just energy.

Many products are boosted with stimulants like caffeine or taurine, or minerals like sodium and potassium.

Electrolyte supplementation can be especially important for any rider going long or going hard. Candy won’t help keep sodium balance in check.

By contrast, candies can include things you might not want in the fueling mix.

Fiber and fats are not your friends if you need fast energy. They slow digestion, and can cause gut rot if eaten during workout intensity.

So, we’re sorry to say it, Snickers fans. That delicious stick of chocolate and nuts might wreck your workout. Save it for when you get home – your stomach will thank you, and your jersey lining might, too. There’s no coming back from finding a melted chocolate bar smooshed into your back pocket after a long or hot ride.

If you want fast fuel, choose your Halloween candy carefully. Nerds Gummy Clusters, Sour Patch Kids, and Skittles will give you more speed than Snickers or Reese’s.

But that’s not to say chocolate doesn’t have a place in your cycling cupboard.

For long, low-intensity rides, chocolate’s satiety and slower-release energy can see you right for endless kilometers. Just ask Oreo and Payday bar afficionado , Lachlan Morton.

But for the sake of your sleek new apparel, consider how you carry it.

And perhaps two of the most obvious considerations when considering gels vs. candy: Portability and munch-ability.

As tasty as Nerds Gummy Clusters might be, anyone who’s tried chewing them down mid-effort is in for a fright. The choking hazard of small candies is very real if you’re trying to hit a workout.

And that’s if you can even access them while on the move.

An easily overlooked benefit of an energy gel is just how easy it is to access and open while you’re clinging to the wheels of the weekend group ride. Ever tried tearing open a packet of Sour Patch Kids with frozen mid-winter fingers while riding 350 watts? Trust us, don’t bother.

A couple of real-food fueling transportation tips?

Pre-open candy packets before you go ride for easy accessibility.

And if you can’t face a six-hour ride without a Twix, we get it. But stash it in the bar bag, not the pocket of your $150 jersey.

Considering some over-age trick-or-treating this weekend?

Here’s how Team Velo ’s favorite candies compare to some leading energy gels to help guide your Halloween ghouling.

We’ve included the costs and total nutritional values of packet sizes often found in a local store, and added our golden metric: cost per carbohydrate.

We’ve also included some reasonable serving sizes for cyclists meticulous enough to split an XL sack of sweets into portions before they ride.

Candy can give you 10 times more carbs per dollar than sport nutrition.

Candy corn worked out as the cheapest of all the grocery store treats, but could you handle the polarizing, waxy consistency?…

items.title: You’ve Heard the Short Crank Hype. Here’s Why You Should Listen.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: I accidentally rode 160mm cranks, and now I’m ruined for anything else. Why everyone should consider going shorter.
items.lbText:
I never set out to sing the praises of 160mm cranks. Having already made the transition from 170mm to 165mm cranks several years ago, I felt like I had reached the promised land of power and performance. There was nothing more to gain. Plus, as a 5-foot-6 cyclist, how much shorter could I reasonably go? Apparently another 5 millimeters.

A lot of times innovations from the pro peloton don’t always make sense for us mere mortals. This one, however, is an exception. Shortening your crank length is a pro move that’s worth paying attention to, because the benefits aren’t just theoretical; they’re practical for riders of all levels.

To get into the details I met with Cesar Correa, founder of San Francisco’s Cassette Fit Studio who has been fitting bikes since 2013, to see why more riders should start to think small. Correa has been recommending shorter cranks for years.

“Crank-wise, I do think it’s very important to go shorter,” he told me. When I rolled into his studio on a Canyon Endurace with its stock 160mm cranks, his reaction was considerably more enthusiastic than mine had been. “When you brought in that bike and we saw that it came with 160s, it was like, that’s amazing,” he says.

Shorter cranks mean shorter virtual circles that your foot is tracing with each pedal rotation. Since your knee doesn’t rise as high at the top of each stroke, you can compensate for this positioning change by bumping up your saddle height.

As a general rule, when you shorten your cranks you raise your saddle height roughly the difference. So if you’re dropping down 5mm from 170mm to 165mm, you would bump up your saddle by 5mm. Give or take.

“That’s the easy way to do it,” says Correa. “But it could add up to about anywhere from eight, sometimes even 10mm different.” Correa says the final adjustment depends on the rider, their biomechanics, and can involve moving the saddle both up and back.

And there’s another catch. “When you move to shorter cranks, you raise the saddle, then some people tend to just drop the handlebars lower, but that means your hips are still going to close,” Correa told me. “So you’re not actually doing anything different.”

So simply going shorter doesn’t give you permission to slam your stem. “You can achieve a bit more drop with the shorter cranks, but it’s not as aggressive as people think.” It’s about creating more room between your knee and torso, which can give you more freedom to find an aerodynamic position without closing your hips back up.

A lower knee raise creates a more open hip angle. But what does that actually mean? The best analogy is a squat at the gym. A closed hip angle is the equivalent of doing a partial squat, which really burns out your smaller hip flexor muscles and doesn’t allow you to produce a lot of power.

Whereas a more open hip angle is akin to doing a full squat—it produces more power and recruits more muscles. From Correa’s perspective, the important part is simply giving your hip and knee more room to move. “When you go shorter in cranks, especially if you have knee issues, your knees are not going to have to bend as much,” he says. “They’re a lot freer.” And it’s something he can actually see during a fit. “Your foot gets through the stroke a lot better with shorter cranks,” Correa says. That extra room can also help the knee track more naturally through the pedal stroke rather than forcing your body to compensate for a position it doesn’t particularly like. For me it just felt more relaxed. Like sitting in a really comfy chair. The body just fell into place and the legs were able to turn over almost effortlessly. I could maintain a high cadence, turning over the pedals without much effort, and ticking up the hills like it was no big deal.

To be clear, shorter cranks don’t magically give you more watts. But the shorter arms change your riding position, and that’s where the magic happens. It all comes down to which muscles you can recruit. And on shorter cranks, you can tap into some big ones.

When you pedal through the power phase of your stroke, between 12 o’clock and 5 o’clock, you can engage your quads more and shift that load into a more efficient power transfer. The short cranks and more open hip angle allow this to happen. Now you’re shifting the load towards your quads, engaging bigger muscles that are more resilient and ideal for endurance efforts. It’s more efficient, more sustainable, and allows you to feel comfortable for longer. I immediately felt this on climbs, like I magically had another gear. I could feel more engagement from my quads, not just my glutes. It’s a little bit of an odd sensation at first, but you quickly get used to it and before long, you’re spinning easier doing some of your most efficient climbing ever.

A 160mm circle versus a 175mm circle is a significant difference, and that means the rotations your foot will make are directly translated. You’ve instantly reduced the arc in which your foot travels across each revolution. It’s a tighter circle which means you can spin faster.

For me, that’s exactly what I noticed on the 160s. Climbing felt easier. My pedal stroke felt quicker, and holding a higher cadence felt more natural than my 165s. And there are other benefits too.

Office workers of the world listen up, this one is for you. “If you’re someone who sits at a desk all day, you’re gonna have the tightest hips in the world,” Correa says. “So shorter cranks will help with that.” Reducing that demand on your hip flexors could also help limit some of the stress that builds up over a long ride. Then there are the knees.

For Correa, watching what happens to the knee at the very top of every pedal stroke is key. “If you can not bend the knee at the top of the stroke as much, that will help, because it’s always that top of the stroke where that bend will cause a lot of issues.”…

items.title: Vollering Betters Pogačar with Near-Perfect Season and More Hot Takes from the Year-End Rankings
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: 2026 women's UCI and victory rankings: Vollering dominates with Giro-Tour-worlds rout, Picnic-PostNL in peril, and what happened to Ferrand-Prévot?
items.lbText:
Demi Vollering just wrapped up the greatest season in the pro peloton.

The Dutchwoman obliterated the women’s UCI rankings with a season-long rout that won her the Giro d’Italia, Tour de France, road world championships, and a whole lot more.

Vollering topped the 2026 year-end rankings with a haul of 9,330 UCI points – some 65 percent more than second-place Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney. Vollering’s Polish nemesis finished the year on 5,660 points.

Spanish super talent Paula Blasi rounded out her breakout season third in the rankings with 5,201 points.

Vollering’s season wasn’t only the best in the women’s road peloton.

It was more impressive than anything achieved on the men’s side of the sport, too.

This year, Vollering strung together a 2026 season even more dominant than Tadej Pogačar’s.

Yes, the Slovenian won the Tour de France for a record-breaking fifth time, unlocked Milan-San Remo, and topped the UCI league by echelons, despite racing for only six months.

He probably would have also won the Vuelta, worlds, and Il Lombardia if a brutal crash didn’t prematurely end his season.

Vollering won two monuments, the world and European titles, and topped the GC of every stage-race she started.

The 29-year-old became only the second woman after Annemiek van Vleuten to complete the triple crown.

And she hit the podium of every one-day road race she started bar Strade Bianche. Being directed off course (depending on your reading of the situation) at the sterrato classic will do that to one’s podium aspirations, we guess.

Vollering’s 2026 season was a masterpiece on-par with anything that GOATs like Van Vleuten, Anna van der Breggen, or Marianne Vos have put together. It was a Hall of Fame eight months that saw FDJ Suez’s superstar leader amass more UCI points than eight women’s WorldTour teams.

Dem Vollering: Rider of the year. Gotta be .

The 2026 UCI rider and team rankings, and a ranking of rider victories, can be found at the bottom of this post.

Here is our breakdown and hot takes from the 2026 men’s rankings.

One thing Vollering didn’t do this year?

But we’ll let her off. Super-mega sprinter Lorena Wiebes was in her own orbit , again.

With a total of 24 victories, Wiebes won the most for the third year in a row. Not even a controversial bike weight disqualification at the Giro d’Italia slowed the 27-year-old’s High Speed Express.

Vollering ranked second in individual wins with 16.

The extent of Wiebes’ and Vollering’s dominance over the Women’s WorldTour is brutally clear if you scan further down the year end victory table.

With “only” 8 and 7 wins apiece, some might think Marlen Reusser and Blasi in third and fourth were riding with brake rub.

Picnic-PostNL’s troubles are not isolated to the men’s peloton.

The under-scrutiny Dutch team is dead-last in the Women’s WorldTour rankings with a total of 2,450 points. That’s 11 percent of the most successful team, UAE L’Imad. The news that long-time leader Pfeiffer Georgi is headed for the exit door will compound Picnic-PostNL’s problems in 2027.

Speaking of UAE l’Imad – the Women’s WorldTour got a new superteam in 2026.

The UAE-based squad topped the UCI charts for the first time courtesy of its prolific leadership trident Blasi, Elisa Longo Borghini, and Dominika Wlodarczyk.

Former dominators FDJ United-Suez and SD Worx-ProTime went two-three, respectively.

But getting to the top ain’t the same as staying at the top.

UAE L’Imad’s winning season might be a one-and-done. Blasi’s blockbuster move to Movistar will blow a hole in her former UAE team in 2027.

Last up – take a look at the rankings again.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot has bombed out of the top 20 after her incredible 2025 season. PFP was woman of the year in 2025 after she won both Paris-Roubaix and the Tour de France femmes.

This year, the template that had worked so well for the Frenchwoman went very wrong, and her form nosedived soon after spring.

Ferrand-Prévot’s year-end ranking of 31st says a lot about her annus horribilis.

But it might not paint the fairest picture.

PFP wasn’t near the top of the board in 2025, either. The 34-year-old races so selectively that she finished only 13th in 2025.

Ferrand-Prévot doesn’t care about points, she cares about history and legacy. 2026 was no doubt a season she’ll be hoping gets lost in the mists of time.

items.title: $85 Million Cost and $130 Tickets: The 2027 Tour de France Grand Départ is Blowing the Budget
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Officials defend controversial charges to Edinburgh team presentation as UK prepares to host 'the most expensive bike races ever' next July.
items.lbText:
The grands départs of the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France are being slated as the most expensive bike races ever held.

British journalist Jeremy Whittle reported last week that the UK government will invest a total of £65m GBP (~$85m USD) into hosting the grands départs of next year’s Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes .

Spanning six days of racing across Scotland, Wales, and England, each stage will cost a staggering equivalent of £11m (~$15m).

And that’s not the only wild expense associated with the Tour’s British start.

The opening ceremony and team presentation of the men’s race will be fully ticketed, with the most premium seats being sold for £99 a pop. That’s just north of $130 for the privilege of seeing Tadej Pogačar and his comrades doing some bemused waving on a big stage.

For race organizer ASO, an overseas start is a lucrative money spinner. It charges host nations millions of Euros for the honor. In return, hosts can use the Tour de France as a promotional platform and legacy investment.

However, next year’s grands départs – the men’s 28th overseas jaunt and the women’s third – will be extraordinary business.

Whittle reported eye-watering expenses associated with the privilege of being the first nation to host a partnered men’s and women’s event.

Running out of Edinburgh on July 2 for the men’s race and from Leeds on July 30 for the Femmes, Whittle called the six stages of the $85m USD carnival “the most expensive bike races ever held.”

For context, the 2014 UK grand départ reportedly cost the British government £29.4m.

While it’s comparing apples to oranges, the full cost of the 11-day multi-format Glasgow “super worlds” in 2023 nudged toward £63m.

But how can a few hundred kilometers of the Tour de France be so costly?

The hosting fees paid over to the race organizer are huge, and they’re only the start.

ASO is thought to have charged around €10m euros (~£8m or $11m) for the rights to host recent grands départ s in Florence (2024) and Barcelona (2026). The hosting charges for 2027 are unknown.

After that, costs associated with staging the biggest bike races in the world include security, road resurfacing, preparing local infrastructure, and supporting all the random side-events that pop up when the Tour comes to town.

The UK Government has projected economic benefits of more than £150m from the combined 2027 men’s and women’s race.

One particular side-event of the 2027 Tour de France has garnered particular interest – and stirred significant controversy – in recent weeks.

The opening ceremony and team presentation of the men’s Tour on Wednesday 30 June will be fully ticketed, and admission ain’t cheap.

Tickets for the event on the esplanade outside Edinburgh Castle span from £27 ($36) for “bring the binoculars” seats high in the stands to £99 ($130) for primo spots.

Pogačar and the peloton will trundle on and off the stage as part of a mash-up ceremony that includes a show by The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo. The traditional Scottish event is a bagpipes ‘n’ kilts show including music, dance, and rock concert lighting.

Details of the Tour de France Femmes opening ceremony have not yet been confirmed.

It’s rare, but not unprecedented, for Tour de France team presentations to be ticketed.

However, the past three, held in suitably spectacular settings in Barcelona, Lille, and Florence, were all free to attend.

News that next year’s team presentation will be ticketed has, of course, stirred debate.

The Tour de France does sell itself on being “the biggest free sporting event in the world,” after all.

When Whittle enquired about the charges as part of his Substack report, a representative argued for the event’s extraordinary nature.

“This isn’t a standard team presentation,” a Grand Départ GB told Whittle. “By partnering with The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, we’re creating a one-off event that fans won’t have seen before at a grand départ, and ticketing reflects that.

“As with any team presentation, the riders will take a route through the city before arriving at Edinburgh Castle, in this case from Holyrood Palace via the Royal Mile to the castle, which will be completely unticketed,” they added.

The representative also reminded Whittle every kilometer of all three stages of the men’s grand départ will be open access.

“The race itself stays free,” they said. “Spectators will have free access to more than 900km of roadside across both grands départs, and we expect people to come out in their millions to cheer on the world’s best male and female riders.”

If the ticket fees aren’t steep enough to put you off the prospect of some traditional Scottish dance and some bemused pro cyclists, tickets go on general sale here on October 30.

items.title: This Is the Future of Gravel Bikes: 6 Bikes Tested Head to Head on a 100km Ride
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: We put our test bikes head to head on a 100km test route from Squamish to Whistler. This route has a little bit of everything, challenging each bike in a different way.
items.lbText:
Our quest to find the future of gravel bikes at the Velo Field Test has taken us on a long journey. We’ve test ridden six bikes that couldn’t be more different on a first impressions loop , and put the bikes through a series of head to head challenges . Now it’s time to test these bikes in the way that really matters: a big ride. In this final episode, we’re riding 100 kilometers (62 miles) up British Columbia’s Sea to Sky corridor from Squamish to Whistler.

In a discipline where people regularly ride hundreds of kilometers in one go, 100 isn’t the most insane distance. But it’s what’s contained in that distance that’s the challenge. Mike Levy has wracked the depths of his local knowledge to devise a course that hits all sorts of gravel terrain, and will push Josh and Logan to their limits as they in turn find the limits of the bikes.

There’s champagne gravel, gravel that is more aptly described as large rocks, steep climbs, technical single track, and some connectors on paved roads for good measure. Each of our six test bikes gets a chance to shine, and will also have its weaknesses glaringly exposed.

We have three riders and six bikes, so in order to test every bike on the ride, each tester will be switching out bikes at the halfway point. Who gets to pick what? Well we settled that in the most obvious way possible: go-karts. We found out that while Logan has Josh beat in a gravel race, Josh’s background hanging around L.A.’s underground street racing scene gave him the upper hand with track times. And that means he gets to pick what bikes Logan rides.

After hundreds of kilometers of riding and a series of head-to-head challenges, Levy, Josh, and Logan sit down to debate what the future of gravel bikes really looks like. Are bigger wheels the answer? Does suspension belong on gravel bikes? Are we sacrificing too much capability in the pursuit of speed? And most importantly, which of these six bikes would each tester actually take home?

The all-rounder: race it or go adventuring.

Specification: Giant Revolt Advanced SL 0, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed: 53mm Weight (tested size): 7.85kg/17.3lbs (ML)

Specification : Factor Sarana, SRAM Force XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.58kg/21.12lbs (Medium)

Specification : Argon 18 Anti Matter + SRAM RED XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 55mm Weight (tested size) : 8.5kg/18.74lbs (Medium)

Specification : Obed GVR, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.12kg/20.1lbs (Medium)

Specification : Pivot Les SL Drop Bar, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission 12-Speed Tire clearance, claimed : 29 x 2.4″ Weight (tested size) : 9.78kg/21.56lbs (Medium)

The 32er. How much difference do big wheels make?

Specification : Salsa Fargo 32 Ti, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission Tire clearance, claimed : 60mm Weight (tested size) : 9.48kg/20.9lbs (Medium)

To settle the debate about the future of gravel once and for all (or perhaps muddy it more than ever), we’ve assembled three test riders who, like the bikes, couldn’t be more different.

Reformed mountain biker turned drop-bar obsessive Mike Levy leads the charge, bringing a technical, rowdy background and a preference for chunkier roads and adventuring far off the beaten path—on Earth and beyond.

He’s joined by Velo’s in-house team of tech editors. Josh Ross likes to ride long distances as efficiently as possible—catch him pedaling all day and night across the gravel roads of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. He’s all about pushing his personal boundaries, and finding the equipment that will help him go the extra mile (or extra 200 miles).

Having once finished 18th overall at the Unbound 200, Logan Jones-Wilkins can’t stop thinking about going fast and squeezing every drop of performance from gravel gear. But when he’s not mixing it up in the pointy end of races, he likes his gravel bike to be a medium for adventuring into the unknown.

That’s three different approaches to gravel, and, naturally, their takes are as varied as the riders themselves. Can they settle their differences and agree on anything? We may have to resort to some good ol’ fashioned tactics to resolve things—which may or may not mean go-kart racing.

To put these bikes to the ultimate test (and the riders too), we’ve taken everyone to the outdoor playground that is Squamish, British Columbia. Finding out the future of gravel means pushing bikes to their limits, so we’ve found a mix of terrain from single track to washboard fire roads to do just that.

We’re stress testing the bikes to get the most possible out of them. In this first episode, we’ve put together a test loop that takes our riders on a smattering of every kind of terrain one might consider gravel, from champagne roads, to loamy dirt trails, to slightly technical, rocky single track, and we’ve got climbing and descending for all of the above.

To keep our testing focused on the bikes themselves, we’ve brought in control tires, 50mm Schwalbe G-One RX tires run at the same tire pressure, mounted to Easton EC90 ALX wheels .

Velo Field Test wouldn’t happen without the support of these sponsors. A big thank you to Endura for providing kits and helmets, Schwalbe for tires, and Easton for wheels!

A special thank you to the crew who made this Velo Field Test a reality!

There’s more to come from the Velo Gravel Bike Field Test! We argue in depth about the future of gravel bikes on our podcast roundtable discussion, plus we have individual reviews for every single bike on test.

items.title: America’s Newest Cycling Team Is Going Large after Breakout Debut Season
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Modern Adventure brings new backing to expand roster with WorldTour talents and national champions as rumors over Quinn Simmons fizzle out.
items.lbText:
Modern Adventure Pro Cycling is sizing up for 2027 after its breakout debut season.

Last week, George Hincapie’s budding team revealed a flood of new signings that will expand its debut roster of 21 riders to 24 for its sophomore year.

WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch, former U.S. national U23 champion Owen Cole, and reigning Australian champion Patrick Eddy all join the team for 2027.

Meanwhile, the exit door has been kept shut. As of late October, no riders have confirmed they will leave the new American team.

Multiple U.S. national champion Quinn Simmons had been repeatedly linked to Hincapie’s ambitious young project. However, the rumor mill has slowed in recent weeks. The 25-year-old’s long-term deal with Lidl-Trek makes any gamble with Modern Adventure seem highly unlikely.

Simmons or not, the arrival of three new riders in 2027 – a 16 percent expansion in the roster – signals clear intent.

In its rookie 2026 season, the team won five times, raced across continents, and saw a marquee invite to Paris-Roubaix.

In 2027, with added financial heft from new co-title sponsor Factor Bikes, Hincapie wants more from a team he hopes to take toward the Tour de France.

“I wanna look back in five, six years from now and go, ‘this is where we started,’” Hincapie told Velo earlier this season. “From basically ‘Bad News Bears’ to building to be one of the best teams in the world.”

Rutsch and Eddy are the household international names of Modern Adventure’s three new signings.

Rutsch spent seven years in the WorldTour and has twice hit the top-11 at Paris-Roubaix.

Eddy rebounded from losing a spot in the WorldTour by outfoxing two Jayco-AlUla riders at Aussie nationals and dominating the Conti circuit with Team Brennan.

Modern Adventure’s biggest hopes might lie with Cole, however.

The 22-year-old Californian won the U23 U.S. road race aged 19, and this year finished top-six in both the national U23 road race and time trial.

Cole spent a year in the UAE Emirates-XRG devo system in 2024 before he reinforced his status as one of USA’s brightest talents in his two years with Team Winston Salem-Flow.

“We’re excited to welcome Owen to the team. He’s a talented young rider with a bright future, and we’re excited to help him develop,” Hincapie said.

“Supporting young, talented American riders is important to us and part of our mission, and we look forward to helping Owen reach the highest level of the sport.”

Cole is the 13th American rider on Modern Adventure’s 24-rider squad for 2027, maintaining its stated mission of having at least a 50 percent American roster.

items.title: The Tour de France Has Made Everyone Angry About a Jersey (Again)
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: The iconic white jersey will get some problematic purple bits to recognize a new sponsor in 2027. The rage is on par with 'green jersey-gate.'
items.lbText:
When the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes revealed their new-look leaders’ jerseys last week, one color caught everybody’s eye.

The iconic white jersey of “best young rider,” last won by Isaac del Toro and Antonia Niedermaier, will get a facelift in 2027.

The typically pearly maillot has been embellished – or some may say, ruined – by an “ultraviolet” purple trim in a nod to the new jersey sponsor, Sanofi. The Paris-based biopharma company has made the lurid purple its “thing,” apparently.

The introduction of “ultraviolet” into the Tour de France palette has become a serious talking point in a cycling world without racing to argue about.

Purple bits are being debated with equal intensity to the 71km of time trialing in the men’s race and a crowning climb – the Puy de Dôme – at the Femmes that might be closed off to crowds.

“A hater has spent years infiltrating ASO and is now taking revenge by ruining one iconic jersey at a time,” is the brilliant title of one Reddit thread on the topic.

Calls of “fashion crimes,” “a Jayco away kit,” and vomit memes are doing the rounds on Twitter / X .

To be fair, not even the mustachioed model looks too impressed in the official marketing shot.

The Tour hasn’t seen this much confab over clothing since … since the last time race organizer ASO made everyone angry with its leader’s apparel.

In 2023, the vert points jersey turned from lime to forest green at the behest of jersey sponsor Škoda.

Couch Peloton has been in protest ever since.

The new maillot blan c of “best young rider” isn’t the only Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes leader’s jersey that will be relaunched next season.

Last week at the official route reveals , ASO revealed tweaked versions of all four of its iconic classification leaders’ jerseys.

The historic yellow, green, polka dot, and white tops have all gotten a refresh for 2027 courtesy of ASO’s new clothing supplier, Castelli.

The Italian brand returns to the Tour for the first time in more than 30 years in 2027. Santini had done the honors since 2022.

Castelli also takes charge of the sewing machine for the ASO-owned Paris-Roubaix, Paris-Nice, Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, and Vuelta a España.

The Tour de France jersey polemica is isolated to just the purple-on-white maillot blanc .

The maillots jaune , verte and à pois haven’t been messed with enough to catch public ire.

In a recent statement, Castelli brand manager Steve Smith paid tribute to the heft of the Tour’s classification jerseys.

“Producing the maillot jaune represents the highest possible honor. We wanted these jerseys to be truly special. That is why every micro-detail stems from our deep reverence for what they represent to the sport and the riders who earn them,” Smith said.

“Beyond pushing performance and aerodynamics, every single feature was crafted to honor that legacy.”

Some may argue purple is not a part of the Tour de France white jersey legacy.

items.title: Remco in the USA: Hanging Out with Fans, Scoping LA Olympics Course
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Time trial superstar Remco Evenepoel already looking to 2028 Games, while Demi Vollering and Kate Courney are also building.
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel has had a interesting off season, visiting the US and also attending the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma in October 11, 2026. (Photo: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto via Getty Images) (Photo: NurPhoto)

It’s the off season, a time to recharge, but that hasn’t stopped Olympic and world TT champion Remco Evenepoel from logging more training kilometers and scoping out the route of a major objective.

The Belgian is currently in California visiting the headquarters of bike sponsor Specialized and has used that time to build relationships and to work on some things which could pay off well in 2027 and beyond.

On Sunday he put in a 65.34km ride, starting near Griffith Park and the LA Zoo, and taking in parts of the TT course for the 2028 LA Olympic Games.

The full route has not yet been released but he still used the time to familiarize himself with the area and with whatever course details he has been able to ascertain.

The ride then concluded close to the beach at Santa Monica.

Evenepoel has been busy since arriving in LA, doing what he described as a LA Jetlag and Sunrise Run on Saturday and then taking in a 48.08km social ride with Specialized.

Photos from the latter were posted by @Shreddypendergrass, and showed Evenepoel doing a group ride in his European road champion’s jersey.

Also present were FDJ Suez riders Demi Vollering and Kate Courtney . The world champ and US national champion are also Specialized-sponsored athletes.

According to Sporza, the trip will see Evenepoel—and presumably the other pros—do additional wind tunnel testing at the Specialized HQ in Morgan Hill.

The Belgian recently spent some days at a Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe training camp, working on plans for next season.

He had his best season to date in 2026, notching up 15 victories including the worlds TT and European championships road race, and taking the runner-up slot in the Tour de France.

Vollering had an even more impressive year, taking 16 wins in 33 days of competition. Her triumphs included the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, the Giro d’Italia Women, the world road championships, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Tour of Flanders and more.

Both are highly ambitious and, like Courtney, are using this time to work towards even bigger results next year.

items.title: The 2027 Tour de France Femmes Route Design Beats the Men’s Race, and It’s Not Even Close
items.author: sstokes
items.content: What the Tour de France organizers got right and got wrong with next year’s two events.
items.lbText:
Demi Vollering won the Tour de France Femmes for the second time this year (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images) (Photo: Tim De Waele)

It lacks high altitude climbs but the route of next year’s Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift does something the men’s event doesn’t do.

The profiles of both races were unveiled Thursday in Paris by organizer ASO. Something that was immediately apparent was that the expected contest between Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard, Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas and others runs the risk of fizzling out days before the conclusion in Paris.

This year stage 20 saw the riders duke it out to the summit of Alpe d’Huez, facing one of the Tour’s most notorious climbs on two successive days.

Pogačar was sufficiently far ahead by then to have the yellow jersey sewn up, but the battle for the podium still raged. Isaac del Toro ultimately distanced Seixas close to the finish and seal third overall.

Next summer? There is a danger of an anti-climax, with the last big mountain battle coming on stage 18’s summit finish at Saint Larry Soulan. The following stage does offer three climbs yet the highest of those, the Col de Soudet, is just 1540 meters above sea level and tops out 65km from the finish.

It is followed by the final categorized climb of the race, the Col de Marie Blanque. It’s a well-known peak, but while it is steep it is just 7.7km in duration and summits a full 18.5km from the finish line.

That’s not exactly a showdown, and the issue is compounded with a sprinters’ day out on stage 20 and a Montmartre-enhanced concluder in Paris which will offer good racing, but may well see the GC neutralized again.

All together, there is a danger the men’s Tour de France could end with a whimper, not a bang.

Fortunately, the same can’t be said of the Tour de France Femmes.

The Femmes race debuted in 2022 and has offered some of the best competition in pro cycling. Just consider the 2024 edition, which was every bit as much a cliffhanger as the conclusion of the men’s 1989 Tour.

Kasia Niewiadoma started the day in yellow, was dropped on the Col du Glandon, but fought all the way to the summit of Alpe d’Huez to win by just five seconds overall.

That was even closer than the classic 1989 showdown where Greg LeMond overhauled Laurent Fignon by eight seconds.

Last year’s race saw Pauline Ferrand Prétot stamp her authority all over the event, easily dropping her rivals in the mountains on the final two days. And while the Frenchwoman did have a 2:37 minute lead going into the final stage, the fact that it was a summit finish meant that there was—theoretically at least—the possibility that Vollering and others could turn things around.

The drama continued this summer when Vollering and Niewiadoma went into the hilly concluder in Nice a mere eight seconds apart.

It was, once again, a nailbiter, and left the outcome undecided right until the finale.

That kind of suspense will continue next summer, thanks to another well thought out route design. The race will again build steadily towards a crescendo, maintaining suspense in a way that the men’s Tour likely won’t.

In trying to avoid another Tadej Pogačar domination, the organizers have neutered things in a way that could backfire.

The Femmes course design avoids that problem. It’s not quite perfect, but it should be very entertaining.

As detailed by Velo’s Andy Hood this week, the Femmes route will begin in Leeds and offers three days of high-stakes racing on British soil. Day one heads to Manchester and takes in 85.7km of rolling terrain. Stage two crams nearly 3000 altitude meters of punchy racing into a 154.4km route to Sheffield, while stage three will be a tricky 18km team time trial in London.

That nervous start will be followed by three complicated transition stages on French soil, to Calais, Magnanville and Bourges respectively. Those offer something for the sprinters, but also for the attackers. Stage 5 in particular could be a puncheurs’ delight, with series of short, steep climbs in the final hour and a half of racing.

The GC battle really comes into focus on the final three stages. Stage 7 is almost completely flat for the first 100km but then concludes with a summit finish to the top of La Loge des Gardes. Sure, the final climb is just 6.7km but it is preceded by a tricky uphill approach which should see some very nervous racing.

Stage 8 is continuously up and down. It does lack a summit finish but 3000 meters of altitude gain en route to Clermont-Ferrand will lead to a lot of tension, particularly if time gaps are tight.

The big decider is stage nine’s summit finish to the top of the Puy de Dôme. The climb is an iconic one, most famous for a literal shoulder to shoulder battle between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor in 1964.

Those slopes were closed to the Tour for many years but made a return to the men’s race in 2023, when Michael Woods won and Tadej Pogačar dropped Jonas Vingegaard, only to lose out overall.

It’s not as long or as tough as other iconic mountains in cycling but everything in the race builds towards this big showdown. And while fans were not allowed on the climb three years ago for the men’s Tour, there are suggestions this could change next summer.

It should be another gripping finale to the Tour de France Femmes, guaranteeing GC suspense right to the closing minutes. It’s something the men’s race should aspire to too yet, next year at least, almost certainly won’t.

That’s a shame for the men’s Tour. At least the Femmes will keep everyone guessing right until the end.

items.title: VIDEO: Tadej Pogačar Slammed for ‘Reckless Riding’ in Monaco
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Viral video showing Pogačar slalom through heavy traffic emerges the day after Tour de France director Prudhomme questions his appetite for risk after brutal crash.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Getty Images / Noah Alfrink Instagram)

Tadej Pogačar heard the Tour de France director questioning his appetite for risk after his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España and said, “Hold my beer.”

Fan footage shot last week showing the 28-year-old slalom through traffic in busy Monaco suggests Pogi has bounced back confident as ever.

The videos, filmed Thursday and shared on Instagram by French amateur Noah Alfrink, are a white-knuckle watch.

The grabs show Pogačar resplendent in his UAE Emirates-XRG jersey cutting lanes, squeezing alongside buses, and flirting with the bumpers of moving cars in the hectic roads of his adopted home.

The videos went viral this weekend and have drawn a very mixed response.

Not even the GOATed fan favorite is spared from criticism of “reckless riding,” a “lack of respect for safety,” and a whole lot more. The 19-year-old Alfrink isn’t shown mercy either, as commentators hit out at the latest example of fans “ cyclo-stalking ” superstar riders.

“I don’t know which is dumber, Pogačar, or the one following him,” reads one comment.

Imágenes de un aficionado siguiendo a Tadej Pogačar durante su entrenamiento de ayer por Mónaco ➡️ El esloveno iba vestido con el maillot del UAE 📹 @noah_alfr pic.twitter.com/fs0nr6sbxI

Only one day earlier, Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme pondered whether Pogačar would be the same after his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España.

The 28-year-old broke his collarbone, a vertebra, and suffered a concussion when he hit the tarmac hard in late August.

It cost the Tour de France dominator the chance to win the Vuelta’s red jersey, defend his titles at the world and European championships, and win a sixth Il Lombardia.

Speaking to L’Equipe on Thursday, Prudhomme questioned whether the crash pierced Pogačar’s sense of invincibility, too.

“The real question for me – and I obviously wish him well – is how well he’ll have recovered from his very, very, very serious crash in the Vuelta a España,” Prudhomme said. “His talent lies not only in his physical superiority, but also in his riding skills.

“His descent of the Tourmalet last summer was mind-blowing and jaw-dropping,” Prudhomme told L’Equipe . “As you get older, after such a massive crash, are you still the same person? Do you take as many risks?”

Prudhomme spoke the day he and ASO unleashed a route for the 2027 Tour de France that’s been labeled “anti-Pogačar.”

The race director suggested 71km of time trialing might not be Pogačar’s only problem when he defends his yellow jersey next July.

“There are certainly questions lingering after his crash,” Prudhomme said. “Whether it has left its mark on him and what the consequences will be.

Pogačar seems to have brushed off any mental hangover of his 60kph crash just fine.

Some may say his comfort on the bike might be a little too good.

Pogačar, his teammates, and the staff at UAE Emirates-XRG meet next for a 2027 planning and admin camp. It doesn’t look like Pogačar will be nervous in the wheels of any group rides.

items.title: Tour de France 2027: What Do Extra TT Kms Mean for Evenepoel’s Prospects?
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Next year’s Tour plays to the strengths of Remco Evenepoel. Could it be enough for yellow?
items.lbText:
Can two time trials in the 2027 Tour de France be the key to victory for Remco Evenepoel? (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images) (Photo: Tim De Waele)

Third in 2024, second this year. Is Remco Evenepoel heading towards victory in the 2027 Tour de France ?

His 6:26 deficit to Tadej Pogačar this time around suggests otherwise, but there are three factors which could narrow the gap considerably.

Firstly, there’s Pogačar’s big crash at the Vuelta a España. He suffered a concussion plus fractures to his neck and shoulder, and was forced to abandon the defense of his world and European championship titles.

While the Tour is still over eight months away, Tour de France race director Christian Prudhomme has suggested that fall might have a long-term effect on the five-time winner.

Correct or not, it’s clear his injuries and his curtailed season were less than ideal.

The second factor is the age gap between the two riders. Pogačar is now 28 and, if he follows the usual pattern seen with many athletes, he could see his performances start to plateau.

Evenepoel is a year and four months younger and, at 26, should continue to improve.

The third consideration is the gift the Tour de France organizers handed Evenepoel this week. Namely, the most time trial kilometers to feature in the race since 2012.

This year’s Tour had just 26.1 individual kilometers against the clock.

Next July will see more than double that, with the two TT’s totaling 71km.

That, plus the fact that there are just three summit finishes, two less than this season, means that Evenepoel will feel good about his chances.

While the Belgian was not at this week’s Tour presentation, his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team gave a big thumbs up to the route.

Directeur sportif Zak Dempster referenced the two races against the clock and said those will help fight for the maillot jaune.

“The first week promises intense racing, where staying out of trouble will be key,” he said.

“The long ITT (individual time trial) at the end of that first week offers us a great opportunity to make an early statement right away. This could be crucial heading into the Alps in the second week.”

And while Evenepoel will then be up against Pogačar and the other favorites in the high mountains, he has a chance to gain further time in the other ITT.

“The second time trial is another highlight of this route,” Dempster continued.

“We welcome the return of more individual time trial kilometers, as this adds another dimension to the race and makes the battle for yellow even more open and exciting. Overall, it’s a route that plays to our strengths and gives us every reason to aim for yellow.”

As for team CEO Ralph Denk, he too was upbeat.

“Remco is the best time triallist at the moment, world champion, and definitely he would be happy. We have two time trials here, more than 70k in TT,” he told VTM Nieuws .

However Denk played down suggestions that three rather than five mountain-top finishes made it an easier Tour in terms of climbing.

“I see this a bit differently because we have a stage of more than 5000 climbing meters,” he said. “It is a super tough one. And there are other climbs here. Let’s see. Let’s evaluate in detail. I will not confirm this is an easy Tour de France.”

“It is always the goal from our team to battle to the best, and let’s see. But for this answer, we need to have a closer look at the route.”

Evenepoel completed the season with a fine statistic. He rode five individual time trials this season, and he won each of them.

He took the TT at the Tour and also won his fourth world championship title, then defended his European champs crown.

He ended off the year with a resounding victory in the Chrono des Nations TT. Evenepoel finished a staggering 2:11 ahead of Jay Vine (UAE Emirates-XRG) there, and said afterwards that everything came together perfectly.

“The handling, the speed and the feeling of being one with the bike all felt really good. Looking ahead to next year, it was all very promising,” he stated.

That kind of performance is why former professional Jan Bakelandts is predicting huge gains in the Tour.

“Remco is genuinely the best time triallist in the world,” he stated in his HLN.be column . “I wouldn’t rule out him taking two minutes out of Pogačar across those two time trials, provided he can reproduce the level he showed at the world championships.

“That’s crucial: he’ll have to be just as brilliant as he was in Montreal, because Pogačar’s track record in the Tour is also astonishingly strong.”

It’s a valid point. Despite Evenepoel’s far greater pedigree as a TT rider, Pogačar limited his losses to 28 seconds in the Tour’s individual time trial this year.

That was over a distance of 26.1km, meaning he gave up just over one second per kilometer.

If he puts in the same kind of performances across the two TTs next summer he will surrender around one minute 11 seconds.

But others such as five time Tour de France winner Bernard Hinault aren’t so sure.

“This Tour is still too hard for him,” he told Nieuwsblad . “This year he has made a nice progression. He had a lower weight and climbed a lot better. But sharp attacks uphill he does not tolerate. Evenepoel is a steady climber. I think he can win stages next year, especially the two time trials.

“But I don’t believe in the general classification. There’s just one that’s better than the rest. And Pogačar will want revenge for the Vuelta.”

Still, Hinault is aware that nothing is guaranteed in sport. He knows pro cycling very well, but also understands that surprises can happen.

“I could be wrong,” he accepted. “And Evenepoel himself must think that he can make it.”

That possibility will sustain the Belgian over the winter months, giving him focus and additional self-belief as he builds towards 2027 and his best Tour prospects thus far.

items.title: Why Flying With a Bike is Always a Gamble (And How to Improve Your Odds)
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: There are no guarantees once your bike disappears on the luggage belt. But understanding TSA habits and airline loopholes gives your frame a fighting chance.
items.lbText:
